summary: Specifies the syntax and semantics for carrying Elliptic Curve (EC) private key information, based on similar definitions from the Standards for Efficient Cryptography Group (SECG). It is informational.

eli5.summary: A private key is a secret number. This says how to write one down in a standard way for a certain kind of math lock, so different programs can read it.

subtitle: A standard ASN.1 wrapper for storing or sending an elliptic curve private key together with its curve and public key.

tldr.problem: Elliptic curve private keys need a common format so that the entity that generates a key pair can hand the private key, its curve parameters and optionally the public key to someone else.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5915 defines the ASN.1 type ECPrivateKey, a SEQUENCE holding a version, the private key as an octet string, the named curve and the public key, normally DER encoded.
tldr.outcome: The structure carries keys inside PKCS #8 or in local files, but it does not protect the key in any way, so it must be combined with a security protocol or encryption.

today: RFC 5915 is an Informational RFC published in June 2010, and no RFC in the unit metadata obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Private Key Format Is Needed
sections.content:
RFC 5915 specifies a syntax and semantics for Elliptic Curve (EC) private key information. That information includes a private key and parameters, and it may also include the matching public key. The design is based on similar definitions from the Standards for Efficient Cryptography Group (SECG).

Most Public Key Infrastructures (PKIs) require keys to be generated locally, but some also support centralized generation, for example by a Certification Authority. The structure lets whoever generates the key pair distribute it together with the associated domain parameters.
sections.eli5: If one person makes a secret key for someone else, they need a standard envelope to put it in, along with a note about which kind of lock it fits.

sections.title: The ECPrivateKey Structure
sections.content:
Computationally, an EC private key is an unsigned integer. For representation, it SHALL have the ASN.1 type ECPrivateKey, a SEQUENCE of four fields.

  • version is set to ecPrivkeyVer1, the integer 1.
  • privateKey is an octet string of length ceiling(log2(n)/8), where n is the order of the curve. It is produced from the integer with the I2OSP primitive from RFC 3447.
  • parameters is the curve. Only the namedCurve choice is permitted, an object identifier that fully identifies the domain parameters. The field is OPTIONAL in the ASN.1, but conforming implementations MUST always include it.
  • publicKey is the matching public key, formatted as in RFC 5480. Implementations SHOULD always include it. It can be left out when the public key is distributed another way, since it can always be recomputed from the private key and the parameters.
sections.eli5: The card has four lines: a version number, the secret number itself, which kind of curve lock it is for, and optionally the matching public number that others may see.

sections.title: Encoding, PKCS #8 and Storage
sections.content:
When generating a transfer encoding, generators SHOULD use the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER), and receivers SHOULD be prepared to handle both DER and the Basic Encoding Rules (BER).

To send a key, the structure goes in the PrivateKey field, an octet string, of a PKCS #8 PrivateKeyInfo (RFC 5208). The algorithm field there names id-ecPublicKey, id-ecDH or id-ecMQV with the named curve as its parameter.

The format can also be used for local storage, although storage is out of scope. One popular choice is PEM: the Base64 encoding of the DER object between -----BEGIN EC PRIVATE KEY----- and -----END EC PRIVATE KEY----- lines. Another is a .der file holding the raw DER encoding. For encrypted keys, ECPrivateKey should be the format of the plaintext being encrypted.
sections.eli5: You can mail the card inside a bigger envelope, or keep it in a file. Writing it in the strict, standard way makes sure everyone reads it identically.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The structure does not protect the EC private key information in any way, so it should be combined with a security protocol. Protecting private keys is vital to public key cryptography. If a signature key is disclosed, unauthorized parties can sign. If a key-management key is disclosed, they can access the managed keying material. The encryption algorithm used to protect the key must be as strong as the key it protects.
sections.eli5: The card is not locked. Anyone who finds it can use your secret, so it has to go into a locked box when you send or store it.
